question: In small-sample, contaminated data-driven decision problems (e.g., a mean-risk portfolio or newsvendor-type problem solved as a convex program), how do credal ambiguity sets (such as an imprecise Dirichlet or epsilon-contamination neighborhood around the empirical distribution) compare with Wasserstein-ball and moment-based (mean-covariance) ambiguity sets in out-of-sample cost and in the reliability of the resulting cost guarantee, as the sample size (n of roughly 10 to 200) and the contamination fraction (0 to 20%) vary, when each set's radius is tuned by the same cross-validation or calibration rule?
why_researchable: All three ambiguity-set families reduce to small convex programs (LP, SOCP or SDP) that a CPU solver such as CVXPY with open-source solvers handles in seconds, so hundreds of replications over n and contamination grids fit on a laptop. Synthetic data with controlled contamination and public return or demand datasets give ground truth for out-of-sample cost and guarantee violation rates. The literature on Wasserstein DRO (finite-sample guarantees, radius calibration) and on moment-based DRO is well developed, while direct empirical comparisons that include credal or contamination-neighborhood sets under matched radius calibration are sparse. A short review can therefore state plainly what theory guarantees (for example, measure-concentration radius bounds that are conservative in practice) and what has not been tested (head-to-head behavior under contamination at small n). The experiment is a bounded comparison, not a claim about general superiority.
candidate_parent: Mohajerin Esfahani and Kuhn, 'Data-driven distributionally robust optimization using the Wasserstein metric: performance guarantees and tractable reformulations', arXiv:1505.05116 (Wasserstein-ball portfolio and newsvendor-style convex reformulations). I cannot confirm from memory that the authors released official public code, so the review should check for it, and otherwise re-implement the reformulations in CVXPY. A moment-based baseline would follow Delage and Ye (2010, DOI 10.1287/opre.1090.0741).
proposed_this_run: In small-sample, contaminated data-driven decision problems (a 10-20 asset mean-risk portfolio and a newsvendor, both solved as convex programs), how do credal ambiguity sets (an imprecise Dirichlet or linear-vacuous contamination set around the empirical distribution) compare with Wasserstein-ball and moment-based (mean-covariance) ambiguity sets in out-of-sample cost and in the rate at which the true expected cost exceeds the robust objective, when a fraction eps of observations is replaced by adversarial outliers and n ranges from 20 to 500?
